Analog Devices breaks every record, but its stock tumbles more than 10%: the chipmaker forecasts a quarter with no growth

On Tuesday, November 24, US-based Analog Devices reported record quarterly revenue of $4.37 billion, above expectations. But its profit forecast for the next quarter came in below consensus, sending the stock down more than 10% before Wall Street opened [1][3][5].
For the August-October quarter, sales reached $4.37 billion, up 42% year on year, against $4.32 billion expected [1][3][5][7].
Adjusted earnings per share came in at $4.06, against $3.89 expected by analysts, according to Investing.com [3].
For fiscal 2026, revenue climbed 38% to $15.2 billion, and $5.4 billion was returned to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks [1].
For the quarter ending January 30, 2027, the group is targeting $4.4 billion in sales, plus or minus $150 million, and adjusted earnings per share of $3.82, plus or minus 20 cents [1][2].

This forecast is below expectations, which were around $3.86 to $3.89 according to the media [4][6]. Before the open, the stock was down 10.5% at $339.01, according to GuruFocus [5]; other readings show a steeper drop [3].
Key takeaway: on the stock market, you buy the future. A record is not enough when the next quarter looks flat, after 42% growth [5].
Analog Devices makes "analog" chips, which turn real-world signals (sound, temperature, electric current) into digital data. They are found in factories, cars, networks and data centers.

Its CEO, Vincent Roche, stresses that "more than two-thirds" of 2026 growth came from markets with no direct link to artificial intelligence, even though AI infrastructure boosted sales to data centers [1]. It is a way of saying the company does not depend only on the AI craze.
The scenario is not new: in May, the stock had already fallen despite a quarter and forecasts that beat expectations [8].

If you hold an index fund tracking the Nasdaq or US tech stocks, these drops after good results keep repeating this fall. They show that prices already reflect a lot of optimism: the slightest disappointment is costly.

How it works: why a stock falls despite good results

A stock's price reflects what investors expect from future earnings. Analysts publish forecasts, and their average is called the "consensus". On earnings day, two numbers matter: the past quarter, compared with the consensus (here $4.06 in earnings per share against $3.89 expected [3]), and the company's forecast for the next quarter, called "guidance". Analog Devices is targeting $3.82 [1], less than the roughly $3.86 to $3.89 hoped for [4][6], and sales of $4.4 billion, barely more than the $4.37 billion of the quarter just ended [1]. Since the price had priced in continued growth, it adjusts downward, even after a record [5].

Seoul falls more than 5%, Taiwan more than 6%: Asian markets slump again as Washington prepares to tax 16 economies over "overcapacity"

On Wednesday, November 25, Seoul, Taipei and Tokyo erased part of the previous day's rebound. On top of persistent doubts about the profitability of artificial intelligence comes Washington's imminent announcement of new tariffs on 16 economies accused of overproducing, including China, the EU, South Korea and Taiwan [1][2][3].
In Seoul, the Kospi was down 5.54% at 4,728.81 points at 11:20 a.m., falling back below 5,000. As early as 9:09 a.m., the exchange triggered a "sidecar", a five-minute pause in program selling [2].
Samsung Electronics fell 9.03% and SK hynix 8.55% during the session. Analysts cite profit-taking and fears of new US tariffs [2].
In Taipei, the Taiex plunged as much as 7.9% in the morning [1], then ended down more than 6%, dragged down by TSMC (−8.1%) and MediaTek (−10%), according to the AP [7].
Only Hong Kong held up, with the Hang Seng gaining as much as 1.3% [1].

According to Reuters, the US Trade Representative (USTR) could publish the findings of its "overcapacity" investigation on November 24 or 25, with new tariffs on a wide range of products. The rates are unknown; a lawyer quoted mentions 15% to 25%, on top of existing tariffs [3].

The investigation, opened on March 11 by Jamieson Greer under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, targets China, the EU, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Taiwan, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Cambodia, Singapore, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Switzerland and Norway [4][6].

Key takeaway: Asia's chip sector moves to the rhythm of doubts about AI, and the US tariff threat adds to it at the worst moment. Wednesday erased part of Tuesday's rebound, sparked by Jensen Huang's return at the head of Nvidia [1].

The mechanism: Section 301 allows the US to tax, with no ceiling, a country whose practices are deemed "unreasonable". For Jamieson Greer, "many trading partners produce more than they can consume at home" [6]. The tool is being used to rebuild Donald Trump's tariff pressure after the Supreme Court struck down his global tariffs [5].

Beijing denounced a "typical unilateral act" as early as March, recalling that the WTO ruled tariffs based on Section 301 illegal [8]. According to the Seoul Economic Daily, the total rate on Korean products would remain capped at 15%, as Washington has promised to honor the existing agreement [9]. Taiwan is waiting: its rate was "not final" in July, said Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun [10].

The European Union is one of the 16 targets: a new tariff would make French products more expensive in the United States. And if your savings include tech or Asian funds, expect sharp swings in the coming days.

Pacific: the Solomon Islands make Australia their "principal security partner", ban all foreign bases and turn their back on the pact with China

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his Solomon Islands counterpart, Matthew Wale, signed a sweeping treaty in Canberra on Wednesday, November 25. The archipelago will host no foreign military base, and Australia is promising 740 million Australian dollars over ten years. Honiara has also reportedly told Beijing it will not renew the security pact signed in 2022 [1][3][6].
The treaty, signed at the Australian Parliament, makes Australia the "principal security partner" of the Solomon Islands and bans any foreign military or security base on their soil [1][3][4].

Honiara will have to consult Canberra before any cooperation on critical infrastructure or security with a country that is not a member of the Pacific Islands Forum. Anthony Albanese did not mention China [1][3].

In return, Australia commits to paying 740 million Australian dollars over ten years, notably to make schooling free [1][2]. It will also support the Solomon Islands police and invest in infrastructure and renewable energy [4].

Albanese promised to publish the full treaty [4], unlike the 2022 China-Solomon Islands pact, which remained secret. That pact allowed Honiara to ask China to send police and troops to maintain order, and authorized port calls by Chinese warships [6][8].

According to the Sydney Morning Herald, cited by Reuters, the Wale government has told Beijing it will not renew this five-year pact when it expires in April. Matthew Wale declines to comment, citing a confidentiality clause [6].

Beijing neither confirms nor denies. On Tuesday, its spokesperson, Mr. Guo, said China develops its relations with the Solomon Islands according to "the principle of mutual respect and equality" [3][4].
Opposition leader and former Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare denounces the "rushed" adoption of the treaty while the fate of the Chinese agreement remains "unclear" [1][2].

Key takeaway: in four years, the Solomon Islands have gone from a secret security pact with China to a treaty that shuts the door on any foreign base. It is a clear setback for Beijing in the South Pacific [1][2].

The 2022 pact, with its Chinese warship port calls, opened the door to a Chinese military presence in the South Pacific [6][8]. An analyst at the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank, speaks of a "massive win" for Australia [5]. The Global Times, a Chinese state newspaper, plays it down: the bilateral relationship does not change as a result [7].

The shift began with Matthew Wale's arrival in office. During his visit to Canberra on June 3, 2026, he announced a review of the agreement with China and the negotiation of a treaty with Australia [9]. Canberra is stacking up such agreements: it had already signed a mutual defense pact with Fiji before turning to Honiara [10].
One uncertainty remains: the Chinese pact only expires in April 2027, and sources differ on whether it has already been terminated or will simply lapse [4][6].

The South Pacific has become an arena of rivalry between China and Western allies. France is directly involved, with New Caledonia and French Polynesia. Each archipelago that picks a side changes the balance of the region.
